questions.q: Which of these is the most precise statement of this course's claim about quantum ML advantage?
options: Quantum ML has been proven mathematically impossible to ever outperform classical ML
Quantum ML already outperforms classical ML on most benchmark datasets
There is no peer-reviewed, independently reproduced result showing a QML method outperforming the best classical method on a real-world task under a fair comparison
No quantum computer has ever outperformed a classical computer at anything
questions.explain: The precise claim is narrow and specific: no proven, reproduced, fairly-compared practical ML advantage exists today -- not a claim that quantum computing never outperforms classical computing at anything (supremacy experiments are a counterexample for a non-ML task).

questions.q: What did Google's 2019 Sycamore 'quantum supremacy' experiment actually demonstrate?
options: Full fault-tolerant, error-corrected quantum computation at scale
A quantum kernel method beating a classical SVM on image classification
A quantum processor sampling faster from a specific, contrived random circuit's output distribution than a classical supercomputer could simulate -- a deliberately non-practical task
A quantum computer outperforming classical ML on a real fraud-detection dataset
questions.explain: The Sycamore experiment used a contrived random-circuit sampling task specifically chosen to demonstrate a measurable quantum-vs-classical computation gap -- it has no practical application and is not an ML result.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the overclaiming patterns the lesson warns you to watch for in QML papers or marketing?
options: Comparing against a weak or outdated classical baseline instead of a strong, tuned one
Ignoring the classical cost of simulating a small quantum circuit
Citing a theoretical fault-tolerant speedup as if it applies to current NISQ hardware
Running the exact same hyperparameter search budget on both the quantum and classical model
questions.explain: Comparable hyperparameter search effort on both sides is exactly what a FAIR comparison requires -- it's the opposite of an overclaiming pattern; the lesson lists it as something a convincing claim SHOULD include, not a red flag.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what would be required for a QML practical-advantage claim to be convincing?
options: A theoretical proof alone, regardless of whether it has been tested on real hardware or data
A single vendor blog post with strong marketing language
A real dataset practitioners care about, a comparably tuned classical baseline, honest total cost accounting, and independent replication by a group without a commercial stake
A demonstration on a toy dataset specifically chosen to favor the quantum method
questions.explain: The lesson sets a high, specific bar: real practically-relevant data, comparable tuning effort on both sides, honest cost accounting (including classical simulation overhead), and independent reproduction -- intentionally strict given how extraordinary the claim would be.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'no proven advantage yet' is not the same as 'QML is worthless'?
options: Because the lesson expects a practical advantage to be proven within the next year
Because classical ML is expected to be replaced by QML regardless of current evidence
Because QML has secretly already been proven to work, just not published yet
Because the course frames QML as valuable for research literacy, transferable skills, and early positioning, with calibrated uncertainty as the correct professional posture
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates 'no proven advantage today' from 'pointless to learn' -- the value is in research literacy, transferable optimization/circuit skills, and being positioned to verify (or debunk) future claims, held with calibrated uncertainty rather than hype or dismissal.
